title: The hunters
text: Two hunters are out in the woods. One collapses and stops breathing. The other calls 911 in a panic. "My friend is dead! What do I do?" The operator says, "Calm down. First, let's make sure he's dead." There's a silence, then a gunshot. "OK. Now what?"

title: Groucho's elephant
text: "One morning I shot an elephant in my pajamas. How he got into my pajamas I'll never know." (Groucho Marx)

title: Doctor, it hurts when I do this
text: "Doctor, it hurts when I do this." "Then don't do that." (Henny Youngman)

title: Dangerfield's second opinion
text: "My psychiatrist told me I was crazy. I said I want a second opinion. He said, okay, you're ugly too." (Rodney Dangerfield)

title: Sherlock Holmes camping
text: Holmes and Watson go camping. In the night Holmes wakes Watson and asks, "What do you see?" Watson says, "Millions of stars. Astronomically, it tells me there are billions of galaxies. Theologically, it tells me God is great. What does it tell you?" Holmes says, "Someone stole our tent."

title: Steven Wright's seashells
text: "I have a large seashell collection, which I keep scattered on beaches all over the world." (Steven Wright)

title: Mitch Hedberg's drugs
text: "I used to do drugs. I still do. But I used to, too." (Mitch Hedberg)

title: Tim Vine's soap
text: "I used to be addicted to soap. But I'm clean now." (Tim Vine)

title: Dangerfield's psychiatrist, two plumbers, and a bartender
text: "I told my wife the truth. I told her I was seeing a psychiatrist. Then she told me the truth. She was seeing a psychiatrist, two plumbers, and a bartender." (Rodney Dangerfield)

title: The economist
text: "An economist is an expert who will know tomorrow why the things he predicted yesterday didn't happen today." (Laurence J. Peter)

title: The dog funeral
text:
A man's dog dies. He loved that dog. He goes to the Catholic church and asks the priest to hold a funeral. The priest says, "I'm sorry, we don't bury animals here. Try the little church down the road. They might do it."

The man says, "Thank you, Father. One more question. Do you think a ten thousand dollar donation would be enough for them?"

The priest says, "Wait. Why didn't you tell me the dog was Catholic?"

title: The parrot in the freezer
text:
A man buys a parrot that swears nonstop. He tries everything. He plays it classical music. He reads it scripture. He shouts at it. Nothing works.

Finally he loses his temper and shoves the parrot in the freezer. The bird squawks and curses for a minute, then goes silent. The man panics and opens the door.

The parrot steps out, shivering, and says, "Sir, I apologize for my language. I've learned my lesson. I'll never swear again." The man is stunned.

The parrot leans in and whispers, "May I ask what the chicken did?"

title: The Pope's driver
text:
The Pope lands in New York, and a limo picks him up. The Pope says to the driver, "You know, they never let me drive. Could I?" The driver can't say no.

The Pope gets behind the wheel and floors it, ninety miles an hour down the highway. A cop pulls him over, walks up, looks in the window, and goes pale. He radios his chief.

"Chief, I've got a problem. I pulled over somebody very important." "The mayor?" "Bigger." "The governor?" "Bigger." "The President?" "Bigger." "Who's bigger than the President?"

"I don't know, Chief. But the Pope is his driver."

title: The talking dog
text:
A man sees a sign in a yard: Talking Dog For Sale, ten dollars. He knocks. The owner points to a lab in the backyard.

The man asks the dog, "Can you really talk?" The dog says, "Sure. I was discovered as a puppy. The CIA flew me around the world. I sat in rooms with heads of state, because nobody suspects a dog. I uncovered three spy rings. Then I retired, got married, had a bunch of puppies, and now I volunteer at the VA."

The man turns to the owner. "That's incredible. Why on earth are you selling him for ten dollars?"

The owner says, "Because he's a liar. He never did any of that."

title: Golf with Moses
text:
Moses, Jesus, and an old man are playing golf. Moses hits into a pond. He raises his club, the water parts, and he chips onto the green. Jesus hits into the same pond. He walks out on the water and chips onto the green.

The old man's drive goes straight toward the pond. A fish jumps up and swallows the ball. An eagle swoops down and grabs the fish. Lightning hits the eagle. The eagle drops the fish onto the green, the fish spits out the ball, and it rolls into the cup. Hole in one.

Jesus turns to the old man and says, "Dad, if you're going to keep doing that, we're not playing with you anymore."

title: Ole's obituary
text:
Ole dies. Lena calls the newspaper to place the obituary. The clerk asks what she'd like it to say. Lena says, "Ole died."

The clerk says, "Ma'am, it's five words for the same price. You have three more."

Lena thinks for a minute. "Ole died. Boat for sale."

title: The head at the bar
text:
A man walks into a bar he's never been to. At the far end, sitting on a stool, is a head. Just a head. No body. The bartender sets a whiskey in front of it like it's the most normal thing in the world.

The man stares. The head drinks the whiskey through a straw. And right before his eyes, a neck grows out from under the chin. Then shoulders. Then a whole torso.

The man turns to the bartender. "What on earth is going on?"

The bartender says, "Oh, that's Eddie. He's a regular. Lost everything in a terrible accident years ago. Then one night he ordered our house whiskey, and something grew back. So he keeps coming in."

The torso orders another. A pair of arms grows out. It picks up the glass with its own hands, finishes the drink, and orders a third. Out come the hips. Then the legs. Then the feet. Eddie is whole again, for the first time in years.

The whole bar goes quiet. Eddie stands up, tests his knees, and grins. He says, "Boys, I'm done. I'm going home to my wife." He walks out the front door, steps into the street, and gets hit by a bus. Dead on the spot.

The man sits there in shock. The bartender just shakes his head, wipes down the bar, and says, "He should have quit while he was a head."

title: Farmer Brown's accident (the trooper)
text:
Farmer Brown is hauling his livestock to market. A cow and a pig ride in the back of his old pickup. Out on the county road, a big delivery truck runs a stop sign and plows right into him. The pickup rolls into the ditch.

Six months later, Farmer Brown sues the trucking company. In court, the company's lawyer stands up, all smiles. "Mr. Brown, isn't it true that right after the accident, the state trooper asked how you were feeling, and you said, quote, 'Never felt better in my life'?"

Farmer Brown says, "Well, yes. But let me tell you what happened." The lawyer says, "Just yes or no, Mr. Brown." The judge leans forward. "I'd like to hear it. Go ahead, Mr. Brown."

"I'm lying in the ditch, hurt bad. My cow is lying next to me, mooing something awful, her leg all busted up. The trooper walks over, takes one look at her, pulls out his pistol, and shoots her right between the eyes.

"Then my pig starts squealing. He's screaming bloody murder, both legs broke. The trooper walks over to the pig, pulls out his pistol, and shoots him too.

"Then he walks over to me, gun still in his hand, and says, 'Sir, how are YOU feeling?'

"And I said, 'Officer, I've never felt better in my life.'"

title: The pig squealed
note: Chip's own joke, and his pick for the best one so far. The model for every story joke here.
text:
Farmer Brown was a hard-working man. Dedicated. Always tending to his responsibilities. But once a year, he'd slip out of the house, leave Mrs. Brown behind, drive into town, and go straight to the bar.

On this particular night, he grabbed his coat and headed for the door. Mrs. Brown said, "Where do you think you're going? You're not going anywhere." He ignored her. He climbed in his old pickup and drove into town.

He drank his fair share. And then some. He was well past the point of driving home. It was late. He got behind the wheel anyway and started down the road.

Boom.

He slammed on the brakes. He'd just plowed into a herd of swine. He looked out at the side of the road, and there lay a big hog. Dead.

Farmer Brown sobered up right quick. He knew this was trouble. He didn't want anybody to know. So he hoisted that hog into the back of his flatbed, got behind the wheel, and somehow made it home. He pulled the truck into the barn, shut the doors, and crept into the house.

Mrs. Brown smelled the liquor on his breath. "Where have you been?" He didn't answer. He passed out cold.

At six o'clock in the morning, somebody's pounding on the front door. Mrs. Brown shakes him. "Wake up. Wake up." He keeps snoring. The pounding gets louder. Then a voice: "Police! Open up!"

Now she shakes him hard. "It's the police!"

Farmer Brown goes numb. He pulls on his overalls, pulls himself together, and opens the door.

The officer says, "Farmer Brown, you're under arrest."

"For what?"

"For murder. At midnight last night, there was a wreck out on Highway 12. A hog was killed."

"It wasn't me, I swear. I don't know what you're talking about. I was in bed, sound asleep."

"You're lying. I can see it in your eyes. Where's your truck?"

"My truck?"

Mrs. Brown raises her voice. "Yeah, Pa. Where's your truck?"

"It's parked in the barn. Where I always park it."

"Let's go have a look," says the officer.

They walk out to the barn and swing open the doors. There's the truck. There's blood all over it. And there's a dead hog in the back.

"Farmer Brown, you have the right to remain silent. Anything you say can and will be used against you."

Farmer Brown hangs his head. He's caught. He looks up at the officer and says, "Just tell me one thing. How did you know it was me?"

The officer says, "The pig squealed."

title: The three envelopes
text:
A new CEO takes over a struggling company. On his first morning, the old CEO, the one who just got pushed out, slides three sealed envelopes across the desk, numbered one, two, and three. "This job will knock you down. When it does, open these. In order."

Six months later, sales slump and the board is restless. He opens envelope number one. It says: "Blame your predecessor." He does. The stock bounces.

A year later, margins shrink and a big customer walks. Envelope number two says: "Reorganize." He does. The press calls him a visionary.

Then the third crisis hits, the worst one yet. He locks his office door and with trembling hands opens the last envelope.

It says: "Prepare three envelopes."

title: The monks and the copies
text:
High in the mountains sits an ancient monastery. For centuries, the monks there have done one sacred job. They copy the holy texts by hand. Day after day. Candle after candle.

A young monk arrives. Bright kid. Eager. After a week, he goes to the old abbot. "Father, may I ask something? We copy every book from the last copy. And that copy was made from the copy before it. If one monk, a hundred years ago, made one small mistake, wouldn't every copy since carry the same mistake?"

The abbot frowns. He strokes his beard. "My son, in six hundred years, no one has ever asked that question."

He takes a lantern and a ring of iron keys. He goes down the stone stairs, deep under the monastery, into the vault where the original scrolls are kept. Nobody has touched them in centuries.

An hour passes. Then two. Then the whole night.

At dawn, the young monk gets worried. He goes down the stairs. In the vault, by the last flicker of the lantern, he finds the old abbot. His robes are torn and his eyes are red. He's banging his forehead against the stone wall and sobbing.

"Father! Father, what's wrong?"

The abbot holds up the ancient scroll with shaking hands and wails, "The word was celebrate!"

title: The green horse
text:
A skinny little cowboy rides into a rough Texas town. He's dusty and tired after two weeks on the trail. He ties his horse to the rail outside the meanest saloon in the county and walks in for a drink.

He orders a whiskey. Then another. He takes his time, maybe an hour.

He walks back outside, and he stops cold. His horse has been painted green. Bright green, head to tail. Mane, saddle, hooves, everything.

The cowboy is furious. He kicks open the saloon doors, marches to the middle of the room, and shouts, "All right! Which one of you no-good, low-down sons of guns painted my horse?"

The whole saloon goes quiet. The piano stops. Chairs scrape.

In the back corner, a man stands up. And keeps standing up. He's six foot eight and three hundred pounds, with arms like fence posts and a scar across his face. He cracks his knuckles, one at a time, and walks slowly over until he's looking straight down at the little cowboy.

"I did," he growls. "What about it?"

The cowboy looks up. Way up. He swallows hard.

"Well, sir... I just wanted to let you know. The first coat's dry."

title: Farmer Brown and Mrs. Brown at the diner
text:
Farmer Brown and Mrs. Brown drive into town for supper at the diner. They're well into their eighties now. He holds the door for her. She takes his arm. They shuffle to a booth by the window.

Farmer Brown orders one hamburger, one order of fries, and one Coke. That's it.

The food comes. Very carefully, he unwraps the burger and cuts it exactly in half with his pocketknife. He counts out the fries, one for you, one for me, until there are two equal piles. He pours half the Coke into a second cup and slides it across the table to her.

Then he starts eating. Mrs. Brown just sits there with her hands folded.

A young trucker at the counter has been watching the whole thing. It tugs at his heart. He walks over and says, "Excuse me, folks. I don't mean to intrude. But please, let me buy the lady her own meal. It'd be my pleasure."

Farmer Brown smiles. "That's very kind, son. But we're fine. We've been married sixty years. We share everything."

The trucker goes back to the counter. He keeps watching. Farmer Brown keeps eating. Mrs. Brown hasn't touched a bite. Her fries are getting cold. The trucker can't stand it. He goes back over.

"Mrs. Brown, please. Your food's getting cold. Let me get you something hot. Why aren't you eating?"

She looks up at him, sweet as can be, and says, "I'm waiting for the teeth."

title: The genie and the bridge
text:
A fisherman is out on a California beach at sunrise. He casts his line, and the hook snags on something heavy. He reels it in. It's an old brass lamp, crusted with barnacles.

He rubs off the sand. Poof. A genie appears in a cloud of smoke. "Master, you have freed me. I grant you one wish. Choose carefully."

The fisherman thinks it over. "I've always wanted to go to Hawaii. But I hate flying, and boats make me sick. So I wish for a bridge. From right here, all the way to Hawaii. So I can drive over whenever I want."

The genie's face falls. "A bridge to Hawaii? Do you know what you're asking? Twenty-five hundred miles of open ocean. Pilings down to the bottom of the Pacific. The concrete, the steel, the storms. That's too much, even for me. Pick something else."

The fisherman thinks again. "All right. Here's my wish. I've been married three times. I've never understood a single one of them. I wish I could understand women. Why they cry. What they mean when they say nothing's wrong. What they really want."

The genie stares at him for a long moment. Then he sighs and says, "You want two lanes or four?"

title: Farmer Brown: look, he's moving
text:
Farmer Brown and two of his oldest friends, Harold and Walter, are sitting in the back row at a funeral. It's the fourth member of their poker group. After fifty years of Friday nights, there are only three of them.

They watch the line file past the open casket. People are saying the nicest things. "He looks so peaceful." "What a generous man." "He'd give you the shirt off his back."

Afterward, the three of them sit out on the church steps in the sun. They're quiet, thinking about it.

Finally, Harold says, "Fellas, when it's my turn, and I'm lying up there in that box, what do you want people to say about you?"

Walter goes first. "I'd like them to say, he was a fine doctor. Forty years of house calls. And a good family man."

Harold nods. "That's nice. For me, I'd want them to say, he was a devoted husband. A teacher who changed young lives. A man who kept his word."

They both turn to Farmer Brown. He's ninety years old and hasn't said a word all day. "Earl? When you're lying in that casket, and people are filing past, what do you want them to say?"

Farmer Brown thinks about it for a long time. Then he says, "I'd like them to say... look! He's moving!"

title: Farmer Brown's hearing aid
text:
Farmer Brown has been deaf as a post for twenty years. The family has given up. At Thanksgiving, the children and grandchildren talk right over him. At Christmas, they talk about him like he's a piece of furniture.

Finally, at ninety-two, he goes to see Doc Henderson. The doc fits him with the newest hearing aid on the market. It's tiny and invisible, tucked down in the ear canal where nobody can see it.

The doc flips it on. Farmer Brown hears the birds outside the window for the first time in two decades. His eyes fill up.

A month later, he comes back for his checkup. The doc tests it. It works perfectly. He hears every word.

Doc Henderson says, "Earl, this is wonderful. Mrs. Brown and the children must be thrilled that you can hear again."

Farmer Brown leans back in the chair and smiles. "Oh, I haven't told them. I just sit in my recliner and listen. I've changed my will three times."

title: The preacher and the cab driver
text:
A preacher and a New York cab driver die on the same day. They arrive at the Pearly Gates together.

Saint Peter looks at his book and calls the cab driver forward first. "Welcome, my son." He hands him a robe of pure silk, woven with gold thread. Then a golden staff. Then the keys to a mansion on the hill, with a pool and a view of the whole of heaven. The cab driver walks off grinning, swinging his golden staff.

Now the preacher steps up. He's beaming. He spent fifty years in the pulpit, every Sunday, twice on Easter. He's thinking, if that cabbie got a mansion, wait until they see what I get.

Saint Peter hands him a plain cotton robe, a wooden stick, and the key to a one-room cabin out by the edge of the clouds.

The preacher is stunned. "Saint Peter, there must be some mistake. I'm a man of God. I preached the Gospel for fifty years. That man was a New York cab driver. He ran red lights. He cursed at everybody. How does he get the mansion?"

Saint Peter closes the book and says, "Up here, we go by results. When you preached, people slept. When he drove, people prayed."

title: The gentle mule
text:
A city fellow buys a little farm in Tennessee. He needs a mule to plow his garden. He drives out to see old Clem, who has one for sale.

Clem walks him out to the pen. "This here's Daisy. Best mule in three counties. Gentle as a lamb. She'll do anything you ask. But you got to ask her nice. Never yell at her. Never raise a hand. Just speak kindly, and she'll plow all day."

The city fellow pays five hundred dollars and leads Daisy home. Next morning, he hitches her to the plow. "Good morning, Daisy. Would you please walk forward?" Nothing. "Daisy, dear, let's get started. Giddy-up, please." Nothing. She just stands there chewing.

He tries for an hour. He tries sweet talk, apples, and sugar cubes. He sings to her. Daisy won't budge an inch. He calls Clem. "That mule you sold me won't move!"

Clem drives over. He looks at Daisy. Then he walks to the woodpile, picks up a two-by-four, and WHACK. He smacks her right between the ears. Then he leans down and whispers, "Daisy, honey, would you please walk on now?" And off she goes, plowing a perfect straight row.

The city fellow is horrified. "Clem! You told me never to raise a hand to her! You said just talk to her nice!"

Clem tosses the board back on the pile. "That's right. But first, you got to get her attention."

title: The smartest man in the world
text:
A small plane is flying over the Rocky Mountains with four people on board. There's the pilot. There's a famous professor, the one the newspapers call the smartest man in the world. There's an old parish priest. And there's a Boy Scout on his way to a jamboree.

Suddenly, there's a bang. Black smoke. Both engines quit.

The pilot comes running out of the cockpit. "We're going down! There are only three parachutes on this plane. I've got a wife and five kids. I'm sorry." He grabs one, throws open the door, and jumps.

The professor leaps out of his seat. "I am the smartest man in the world! My mind belongs to humanity! The world cannot afford to lose me!" He snatches a pack, and out the door he goes.

Now it's just the old priest and the Boy Scout. The wind is howling through the open door. The plane is diving.

The priest puts a hand on the boy's shoulder. "Son, I've lived a long, full life. I've made my peace with God. You have your whole life ahead of you. Take the last parachute. Go."

The Boy Scout says, "Relax, Father. There are still two parachutes. The smartest man in the world just jumped out with my backpack."

title: Mrs. Brown on the interstate
text:
A state trooper is parked in the median on I-75, running radar. Farmer Brown's big old Buick comes flying past at eighty-five miles an hour, weaving a little. And Farmer Brown isn't driving it.

The trooper hits the lights and the siren and takes off after it. He pulls up alongside, ready to wave the driver over.

He looks in the window, and he can't believe his eyes. Behind the wheel is Mrs. Brown, eighty if she's a day. Blue hair. Pearls. And she's got two knitting needles going, click, click, click, with a ball of yarn in her lap, steering with her knees.

The trooper flashes his lights. She doesn't notice. He blasts the siren. Nothing. Click, click, click.

So he rolls down his window, gets right up next to her, and yells as loud as he can, "PULL OVER!"

Mrs. Brown looks over, smiles sweetly, holds up her knitting, and shouts back, "NO! SOCKS!"

title: Stung on the golf course
text:
It's Saturday morning at the country club. Old Doc Henderson, a retired surgeon, is sitting at the bar in the clubhouse, nursing a Bloody Mary.

The door bursts open. In hobbles Frank, one of the regulars. He's red-faced, limping, and grimacing with every step. He drops onto the stool next to the doc. "Doc, you've got to help me. I've had the worst morning of my life."

"What happened, Frank?"

"I'm on the first tee. Beautiful drive, right down the middle. I'm walking up the fairway, feeling great. All of a sudden, a bee flies right up my pant leg. I'm hopping around, swatting at it, and the darn thing stings me."

The doc sets down his drink. "Oh, that's no good. Where'd it get you?"

Frank lowers his voice. "Between the first and second hole."

The doc thinks about that for a moment. Then he picks his drink back up, takes a sip, and says, "Well, Frank. Sounds like your stance is too wide."

title: Ole goes ice fishing
text:
It's January in Minnesota, twenty below. Ole decides he's going ice fishing. He loads up his auger, his bucket, his bait, and a thermos of coffee, and heads out.

He finds a nice flat spot on the ice and gets down on his knees. He starts cranking the auger. Grind, grind, grind.

Suddenly, a deep voice booms from above: "THERE ARE NO FISH UNDER THE ICE."

Ole freezes. He looks around. Nobody's there. He shrugs it off, picks up his gear, moves twenty feet over, and starts drilling again. Grind, grind, grind. "THERE ARE NO FISH UNDER THE ICE."

Now Ole is scared. His hands are shaking. He moves all the way to the other side, gets down, and starts drilling one more time. "I SAID, THERE ARE NO FISH UNDER THE ICE."

Ole drops the auger. He looks straight up toward heaven, takes off his hat, and whispers, "Lord? Is that you?"

And the voice booms back, "No. This is the manager of the hockey rink."

title: Farmer Brown and the city lawyer
text:
One fall morning, Farmer Brown is out mending fence along his back pasture. Across the creek, he sees a shiny black SUV parked by the road. A big-city lawyer is out duck hunting, decked out in brand-new gear with the tags still on the jacket.

Bang. The lawyer drops a fat mallard. It tumbles out of the sky and lands smack in the middle of Farmer Brown's pasture.

The lawyer climbs over the fence and starts marching across the field to get it. Farmer Brown sets down his hammer and walks over to meet him. "Morning. That's my land you're standing on."

"I shot that duck. It's my duck. And I'm an attorney. If you don't let me take it, I'll sue you for everything you own. Your farm, your truck, your cows. Everything."

Farmer Brown scratches his chin. "Well, sir. You ain't from around here. Out here, we settle these things the old way. The three-kick rule. I kick you three times. Then you kick me three times. Back and forth, till somebody gives up. Last man standing gets the duck."

The lawyer looks him over. Farmer Brown is seventy-two years old and skinny as a fence post. The lawyer figures this will be easy. "Fine. Let's go."

Farmer Brown steadies himself. His first kick, with a steel-toed boot, lands square on the lawyer's shin. The lawyer howls. The second kick lands right in his backside, and the lawyer goes flying face down into the cow pasture. The third kick catches him in the ribs as he's trying to get up.

The lawyer lies there groaning for a good five minutes. Finally, he staggers to his feet, covered in mud and worse, and snarls, "All right, old man. Now it's my turn."

Farmer Brown tips his hat. "Nah. I give up. You can have the duck."

title: Farmer Brown and the federal inspector
text:
One hot July afternoon, a government sedan comes rattling up Farmer Brown's gravel drive. Out steps a young man in a pressed suit and shiny shoes, clipboard in hand. "Mr. Brown? I'm with the Department of Agriculture. I'm here to inspect your property."

Farmer Brown wipes his hands on his overalls. "Well, all right. Look around all you want. Just don't go in that far pasture, past the red gate."

The inspector puffs up his chest. He pulls out a leather wallet and flips open a shiny gold badge. "Mr. Brown, do you see this badge? This badge is issued by the United States government. This badge means I can go anywhere I want, on any property I want, any time I want. I don't need your permission. Is that understood?"

Farmer Brown nods. "Yes, sir. Understood." He goes back to fixing his tractor.

Twenty minutes later, Farmer Brown hears screaming. He looks up. There's the inspector, running across the far pasture as fast as his shiny shoes will carry him. His clipboard is gone and his tie is flapping. Right behind him, snorting and gaining with every step, is Farmer Brown's two-thousand-pound prize bull.

The inspector screams, "HELP ME! HELP ME!"

Farmer Brown drops his wrench, runs to the fence, cups his hands around his mouth, and yells, "YOUR BADGE, SON! SHOW HIM YOUR BADGE!"

title: Farmer Brown's three-legged pig
text:
A salesman from the city is driving the back roads, selling tractor parts. He pulls into Farmer Brown's place. Farmer Brown is on the porch with a glass of sweet tea, and he waves him up to sit a spell.

While they're talking, the salesman notices a pig trotting around the yard. It's a big, healthy pig, but it has a wooden leg. It hobbles along, clump, clump, clump. "Mr. Brown, I have to ask. What's the story with that pig?"

Farmer Brown sets down his tea. "Son, that is the finest pig that ever lived. Two winters ago, I was out on the pond, and the ice gave way. I went under. That pig ran out on the ice, grabbed my collar in his teeth, and dragged me out. Saved my life."

"That's amazing."

"Oh, that ain't all. Last spring, the house caught fire in the middle of the night. That pig busted through the screen door, squealing his head off, woke up me and Mrs. Brown, and dragged both our grandbabies out of the back bedroom. Saved the whole family."

"Incredible. But what about the wooden leg?"

Farmer Brown leans over and pats the salesman on the knee. "Son. A pig that good, you don't eat all at once."

title: Farmer Brown's airplane ride
text:
Every year, Farmer Brown and Mrs. Brown go to the county fair. And every year, out by the livestock barns, there's a fellow with an old open-cockpit biplane, selling rides for ten dollars a head.

And every year, Farmer Brown says, "Ma, I'd sure like to ride in that airplane." And every year, Mrs. Brown says, "Pa, ten dollars is ten dollars." This goes on for twenty years.

Finally, the year Farmer Brown turns eighty, he plants his feet in front of that biplane. "Ma, I'm eighty years old. If I don't ride that airplane this year, I never will." Mrs. Brown says, "Pa, ten dollars is ten dollars."

The pilot has been listening to this for twenty years. He walks over. "Folks, I'll make you a deal. I'll take you both up. If you can sit through the whole ride without saying one single word, the ride is free. But if either of you makes a sound, you pay me twenty dollars."

Mrs. Brown thinks it over. "Deal."

Up they go. The pilot throws everything he's got at them. Loop-the-loops. Barrel rolls. Flying upside down. A nose dive straight at the cornfield, pulling up at the last second. There's not a peep from the back seat.

He lands, taxis up, and turns around, amazed. "Mr. Brown, I've been flying thirty years. I've never seen anything like it. You didn't say one word."

Farmer Brown says, "Well, I'll be honest with you. I almost said something when Ma fell out. But ten dollars is ten dollars."

title: Farmer Brown and the outhouse
text:
Back when Farmer Brown was a young man, he and Mrs. Brown had a boy named Junior. Ten years old. All elbows and mischief. The farm had no indoor plumbing yet, just an old wooden outhouse perched on the bank above the creek.

Junior hated that outhouse. Cold in winter. Hot in summer. Spiders everywhere.

One spring morning, the creek is running high from the rains. Junior sneaks down, puts his shoulder to the back wall of the outhouse, and pushes. It creaks. It tips. And over it goes, tumbling down the bank, splash, into the creek. It floats away downstream.

That evening at supper, Farmer Brown sets down his fork. "Somebody pushed the outhouse into the creek. Who did it?"

Silence. Mrs. Brown looks at Junior. Junior looks at his plate.

Now, that very week at school, the teacher had told the class about young George Washington. How he chopped down his father's cherry tree. How his father asked who did it. And how George said, "Father, I cannot tell a lie. I did it." And his father was so proud of his honesty, he didn't punish him at all.

So Junior stands up, puts his hand over his heart, and says, "Pa, I cannot tell a lie. I pushed the outhouse into the creek."

Farmer Brown stands up. He slowly unbuckles his belt. "Son, come with me to the woodshed."

"But Pa! Teacher said when George Washington told the truth, his father didn't punish him!"

Farmer Brown says, "That's true, son. But George Washington's father wasn't in the cherry tree."

title: Farmer Brown and the consultant
text:
Farmer Brown is out in his pasture one morning, leaning on the gate, watching his sheep graze.

A brand-new silver BMW comes flying down the dirt road and skids to a stop in a cloud of dust. Out steps a young man. Italian suit. Designer sunglasses. Bluetooth thing in his ear. Shoes that cost more than Farmer Brown's tractor.

He strides up to the fence. "Morning, old-timer. I'll make you a bet. If I can tell you exactly how many sheep you've got in that pasture, will you give me one?"

Farmer Brown looks him over. Looks at the flock. "Sure. Why not."

The young man pulls out his laptop. He connects it to his phone, pulls up satellite images of the pasture, and runs some software. He opens a spreadsheet with about three hundred rows and types furiously for twenty minutes. Then he prints out a forty-page report on a little printer in his trunk, complete with charts and graphs.

He hands it over with a flourish. "You have exactly one thousand, five hundred and eighty-six sheep."

Farmer Brown flips through the report. "Well, I'll be. That's exactly right. A deal's a deal. Go pick one out."

The young man walks into the pasture, picks one up, and loads it into the back seat of his BMW.

Farmer Brown says, "Now hold on, son. Let me make you a bet. If I can tell you exactly what you do for a living, will you give it back?"

The young man laughs. "Sure, old man. Go ahead."

"You're a consultant."

The young man's jaw drops. "That's amazing! How did you know?"

Farmer Brown says, "Easy. Nobody called you. You showed up anyway. You charged me for telling me something I already knew. And you don't know a thing about my business. Now give me back my dog."

title: Farmer Brown goes to New York
text:
Farmer Brown and Mrs. Brown decide to take their first real vacation in forty years. Two weeks in Europe. They're flying out of New York City.

So Farmer Brown drives the old pickup all the way to Manhattan. Rusted fenders. One headlight. Hay in the bed. Chickens' feathers still stuck to the tailgate. He pulls right up in front of the biggest bank on Wall Street.

He walks in, still in his overalls and his John Deere cap, and asks to see a loan officer. A slick young banker comes out, looks him up and down, and tries not to laugh.

"How can I help you, sir?"

"I'd like to borrow five thousand dollars. For two weeks."

The banker smirks. "And what do you have for collateral?"

Farmer Brown hands him the keys. "My truck. It's parked right out front."

The banker looks out the window at the old pickup. He chuckles. But he does the paperwork, approves the loan, and has a valet drive the truck down into the bank's private underground garage. As soon as Farmer Brown leaves, the whole office has a good laugh. "Did you see that? A farmer borrowing five grand against that heap."

Two weeks later, Farmer Brown comes back, tanned and rested. He pays back the five thousand dollars, plus interest. Fifteen dollars and forty-one cents.

The banker says, "Mr. Brown, while you were gone, we ran a background check. It turns out you own four thousand acres of farmland, three grain elevators, and a big stake in the local bank back home. You're worth about forty million dollars. Why on earth would you need to borrow five thousand dollars?"

Farmer Brown takes his keys and smiles.

"Son, where else in New York City can I park for two weeks for fifteen dollars?"

title: Farmer Brown's sick horse
text:
One morning, Farmer Brown's old horse, Buck, won't get up. He's lying in his stall, groaning. Farmer Brown calls the vet.

The vet comes out, examines Buck, and shakes his head. "Earl, it's a bad virus. I'll leave you some medicine. Give it to him for three days. If he's not up on his feet by the third day, we'll have to put him down."

Now, the pig is in the next pen over, listening to the whole thing.

Day one. Farmer Brown gives Buck the medicine. Buck just lies there. As soon as Farmer Brown leaves, the pig trots over to the stall. "Come on, Buck. Get up. You can do it."

Buck groans. "I can't. I'm too tired."

Day two. More medicine. Still nothing. The pig comes over again. "Buck, listen to me. Tomorrow's the third day. You heard the vet. If you don't get up, they're going to put you down. Come on, buddy. Get up!"

Buck lifts his head. Then lets it fall again.

Day three. Farmer Brown gives Buck the last of the medicine. The vet's truck is coming up the drive. The pig runs to the stall, frantic. "Buck! This is it! The vet's here! Get up! Get UP! You can do it! Come on, come on, come on!"

And with a great heave, Buck staggers to his feet. Then he trots out of the barn. Then he breaks into a gallop, racing around the pasture, tail high, kicking up his heels.

Farmer Brown runs out of the house, yelling, "Ma! Ma, come quick! It's a miracle! Buck is up and running!

This calls for a celebration. Let's kill the pig!"

title: Farmer Brown's last cookie
text:
Farmer Brown is ninety-one years old, and he's dying. He's lying in the big bed upstairs, under the quilt Mrs. Brown made the year they married. The doctor has come and gone. The family has said their goodbyes. It's only a matter of hours.

He drifts in and out. And then, from somewhere downstairs, a smell floats up through the floorboards. Warm butter. Brown sugar. Chocolate.

Mrs. Brown's chocolate chip cookies. The best in the county. Seventy years he's been eating those cookies.

Farmer Brown opens his eyes. He thinks, if I'm going, I'm going with one of those cookies.

He gathers every ounce of strength he has left. He rolls out of bed and drops to the floor. He crawls across the bedroom. He drags himself to the top of the stairs. One step at a time, he slides down, gasping, all the way to the bottom. He crawls down the hallway and into the kitchen.

And there, on the kitchen table, cooling on wax paper, are three dozen of Mrs. Brown's chocolate chip cookies.

With his last bit of strength, he pulls himself up on a chair. His hand trembles. He reaches out. His fingers touch a warm cookie...

WHACK. Mrs. Brown smacks his hand with a spatula.

"Pa! Leave those alone.

They're for the funeral."

title: Mrs. Brown's duck
text:
Mrs. Brown has a pet duck named Petunia. She raised it from a duckling. It follows her around the yard. It sleeps in a basket by the stove. Farmer Brown says she loves that duck more than she loves him. Mrs. Brown has never denied it.

One morning, Petunia doesn't get up. She's lying in her basket, stiff as a board.

Mrs. Brown wraps her in a dish towel, makes Farmer Brown drive her to town, and marches into the veterinarian's office. "Doctor, something's wrong with Petunia. Please help her."

The vet lays the duck on the table. He puts his stethoscope to her chest. He listens for a long time. Then he looks up. "Mrs. Brown, I'm so sorry. Your duck has passed away."

"No! She can't be! I want a second opinion. I want tests. I want everything!"

The vet sighs. He goes into the back room and comes out with a big black Labrador retriever. The Lab walks up to the table, puts his front paws up, and sniffs the duck from beak to tail. Then he looks at Mrs. Brown, shakes his head sadly, and walks out.

Then the vet goes back again and comes out with a cat. The cat jumps up on the table. It walks slowly around the duck, sniffing, three full circles. Then it looks at Mrs. Brown, shakes its head, and hops down.

The vet says, "Mrs. Brown, I'm very sorry. The duck is dead." He prints out the bill and hands it to her.

Mrs. Brown looks at it. "One hundred and fifty dollars? Just to tell me my duck is dead?"

Farmer Brown nearly falls out of his chair.

The vet says, "Ma'am, if you'd taken my word for it, it would have been twenty dollars. But with the Lab report and the cat scan..."

title: Farmer Brown's chainsaw
text:
Every fall, Farmer Brown cuts firewood for the winter. Forty years he's done it the same way. A double-bit axe and a crosscut saw. Ten trees a week, if his back holds out.

This year, the salesman down at the hardware store gets ahold of him. "Earl, it's time you joined the twentieth century. This here is the brand-new Thunder King. Top of the line. Guaranteed to cut fifty trees a day. If it doesn't, bring it back and I'll refund every penny."

Fifty trees a day. Farmer Brown pays six hundred dollars cash and drives home grinning.

Next morning, he's out in the woodlot at sunrise. He works all day long. He's sweating, grunting, his arms are shaking. When the sun goes down, he counts. Twelve trees.

Well, he figures, I'm just new at this. Next day, he starts at four in the morning, works by lantern light until ten at night. He doesn't stop for lunch. He doesn't stop for supper. He counts. Twenty trees.

Third day, Mrs. Brown packs him three meals. He works from three in the morning until midnight. He's half dead. He counts. Twenty-three trees.

Next morning, Farmer Brown storms into the hardware store and slams the Thunder King down on the counter. "This thing's a lemon. I near killed myself. Twenty-three trees, best day. I want my money back."

The salesman frowns. "That's strange. Let me take a look." He sets the saw on the floor, grabs the cord, and gives it a big pull.

VROOOOM!

Farmer Brown jumps back three feet. "WHAT IN TARNATION IS THAT NOISE?"

title: Paddy O'Toole and the three pints
text:
In a little pub in County Clare, a fellow named Paddy O'Toole comes in every evening at six o'clock, regular as the church bell. He sits at the end of the bar, and he orders three pints of Guinness. Not one. Three.

He drinks a sip from the first. Then a sip from the second. Then a sip from the third. Round and round, until all three are gone. Then he orders three more.

After a few weeks of this, the barman, Declan, can't stand it any longer. "Paddy, it's none of my business. But why three pints at once? You know they'd be fresher if you had them one at a time."

Paddy sets down his glass. "Ah, it's my brothers, you see. There were three of us lads. Rory went off to Boston. Finn went off to Sydney. And I stayed here at home. Before we parted, we made a promise. Every evening, each of us would drink a pint for the other two. So that way, we'd always be drinking together."

Declan is touched. He tells the story all over the village. Before long, the whole pub knows it. Paddy and his three pints become a fixture. People raise a glass to the O'Toole brothers.

Then one evening, Paddy comes in at six o'clock, sits at the end of the bar, and orders just two pints.

The whole pub goes quiet. Everyone knows what it means. Declan sets down the two pints, reaches over, and puts a gentle hand on Paddy's shoulder.

"Paddy, I'm so sorry for your loss. Which one was it? Rory or Finn?"

Paddy looks up, puzzled. "Ah, no, no. Rory and Finn are grand, the both of them.

It's me. I've quit drinking. So I'm just here with my brothers."
note: Punchline is Chip's: "I've quit drinking. So I'm just here with my brothers."

title: Lord Hargreaves and the butler
text:
Lord Hargreaves of Hargreaves Hall is a proper English gentleman. Tweed jacket. Clipped moustache. Four hundred years of family portraits on the walls. And for thirty years, he has been served by the same loyal butler, Jenkins.

One afternoon, His Lordship comes home from London a day early. He hands Jenkins his hat and umbrella, and without a word, he marches straight up the grand staircase to Her Ladyship's bedroom.

A moment later, the bell rings. Jenkins climbs the stairs and appears at the bedroom door. "You rang, my lord?"

Lord Hargreaves is standing by the window, his back to the room. He doesn't turn around.

"Jenkins. Close the door."

"Very good, my lord." Jenkins closes the door.

"Jenkins. Take off Her Ladyship's dress."

Jenkins hesitates. Then, slowly and with great care, he takes off Her Ladyship's silk evening dress.

"Now, Jenkins. Take off Her Ladyship's stockings."

A long pause. Jenkins clears his throat. "Very good, my lord." Off come the stockings.

"And now, Jenkins. Her Ladyship's pearls."

Jenkins takes off the pearls and lays them on the dresser. He stands perfectly still, staring straight ahead.

Lord Hargreaves turns around slowly and fixes him with an icy stare.

"Jenkins. If I ever catch you wearing my wife's clothes again, you're sacked."

title: The preacher's horse
text:
The new Baptist preacher in town needs a horse to ride out to his country churches. Somebody tells him Farmer Brown has one for sale. So the preacher drives out to the farm.

Farmer Brown leads out a fine chestnut mare. "Reverend, this here is Grace. Best horse I ever raised. But you need to know something. I trained her a little different. She don't go on 'giddy-up.' She don't stop on 'whoa.' To make her go, you say, 'Praise the Lord.' To make her stop, you say, 'Amen.'"

The preacher smiles. "Mr. Brown, I believe that horse was meant for me."

He pays, climbs in the saddle, and says, "Praise the Lord." Grace starts walking. "Praise the Lord, praise the Lord!" She breaks into a trot. "PRAISE THE LORD!" And off she goes at a full gallop, across the pasture, down the road, up into the hills.

The preacher is having the time of his life. Wind in his face. Coattails flying. And then he looks up.

Straight ahead, not two hundred yards away, is the edge of a cliff. A sheer drop, five hundred feet down to the river.

He panics. He pulls the reins. "Whoa! Whoa, Grace! WHOA!" She keeps galloping. What was the word? What was the word?

One hundred yards. Fifty yards. He squeezes his eyes shut and starts to pray. "Dear Lord, forgive me my sins, and receive me into Your kingdom. Amen."

Grace skids to a stop. Her front hooves are right on the edge of the cliff. Pebbles tumble over and fall, and fall, and fall.

The preacher opens his eyes. He looks down at that five-hundred-foot drop. He lets out a long breath, wipes the sweat from his brow, raises both hands to heaven, and shouts,

"PRAISE THE LORD!"

title: Paddy O'Toole's confession
text:
Paddy O'Toole works on a building crew in Galway. Thirty years he's been a carpenter. Good with his hands. Not so good with his conscience.

One Saturday evening, he shuffles into Saint Brigid's, kneels down in the confession box, and the little wooden window slides open.

"Bless me, Father, for I have sinned. It's been, ah, a good while since my last confession."

Father Flanagan sighs. "Go on, Paddy."

"Father, I've been taking a bit of lumber from the job site. Just a board here and a board there. Nobody misses it."

"I see. And how much lumber are we talking about, Paddy?"

"Well, Father. Enough to build a doghouse for the dog."

"Mm-hmm."

"And a henhouse for the hens."

"Go on."

"And a garden shed. And a new back porch. And a garage for the car. And, ah, two bedrooms on the back of the house for the grandchildren."

There's a long silence on the other side of the screen.

"Paddy, that's a very serious sin. For your penance, I want you to make a supplication. Do you know how to make a supplication?"

"No, Father, I can't say that I do.

But if you've got the plans, I've got the lumber."

title: Sister Mary Margaret runs out of gas
text:
Sister Mary Margaret works as a visiting nurse in the hills of north Georgia. Every day she drives her little old Ford from farmhouse to farmhouse, checking on the sick and the shut-ins.

One afternoon, coming down a long country road, the engine sputters, coughs, and dies. She's out of gas.

Luckily, there's a filling station about a mile back. She walks there in her habit, in the July heat. But when she gets there, the attendant shakes his head. "Sorry, Sister. Somebody borrowed my only gas can and never brought it back. I've got nothing to put it in."

Sister Mary Margaret thinks a moment. Then she remembers. In the trunk of her car, she has her nursing supplies. Bandages, a thermometer, and a clean bedpan.

So she walks the mile back to the car, gets the bedpan, walks the mile back to the station, and has the man fill it up with gasoline. Then she walks the mile back again, very carefully, holding that sloshing bedpan out in front of her with both hands.

Just as she gets to her car, a pickup truck pulls onto the shoulder behind her. Two good old boys in feed caps are sitting in the cab, watching.

Sister Mary Margaret unscrews the gas cap. She lifts the bedpan, tips it, and starts pouring it into the tank.

The two old boys stare. They don't say a word. Their mouths are hanging open.

Finally, the driver turns to his buddy and says,

"Bubba, I'm telling you right now. If that car starts, I'm turning Catholic."

title: Mrs. Brown and the Governor
text:
It's an election year, and the Governor is working the back roads, shaking every hand in the county. On Sunday, he shows up at the First Baptist Church homecoming supper, right after the morning service.

The church ladies have outdone themselves. Long tables under the oak trees. Fried chicken. Deviled eggs. Butter beans. Biscuits still steaming from the oven.

The Governor gets in line with his paper plate, smiling and nodding. At the end of the table stands Mrs. Brown, in her Sunday hat and apron, with a dish of butter and a little knife. One pat of butter on every biscuit.

The Governor holds out his plate. Mrs. Brown puts one pat of butter on his biscuit.

He smiles. "Ma'am, could I trouble you for one more pat?"

"Sorry. One pat per person."

He chuckles. "Ma'am, I don't think you understand. I'd like two pats of butter."

Mrs. Brown doesn't move. "One pat per person."

The Governor's smile tightens. He leans in. "Ma'am, do you know who I am? I'm the Governor of this state. I command the State Police. I sign the budget. I appoint the judges. I have the power to pardon a man on death row."

Mrs. Brown looks him dead in the eye.

"And do you know who I am?"

"No, ma'am. Who are you?"

"I'm the lady in charge of the butter. Move along."

title: Paddy O'Toole's last wish
text:
Forty years after his famous confession, Paddy O'Toole is the richest builder in all of Galway. Houses, shops, a hotel, half the new church. Some say it was all built on that first stack of borrowed lumber. Paddy has never denied it.

Now he's eighty-eight, and he's dying. The whole family is gathered around the big bed. Father Flanagan, very old himself now, has given him the last rites.

Paddy opens his eyes and whispers, "Fetch me my solicitor. And fetch me my banker."

The family is puzzled. But they send for them. Within the hour, in comes his solicitor, Mr. Doyle, in his pinstripe suit. Then his banker, Mr. Kavanagh, with his leather briefcase.

Paddy waves a weak hand. "Doyle, you sit on that side of the bed. Kavanagh, you sit on this side."

The two men sit down, one on each side. Paddy closes his eyes. He folds his hands on his chest. He smiles, peaceful as a summer evening.

The room is silent. Minutes pass.

Finally, Father Flanagan leans in. "Paddy. Is there something you'd like to say? Something you want these men to do for you?"

Paddy opens one eye.

"No, Father. It's just that Our Lord died between two thieves. And I thought I'd go the same way."

title: Paddy O'Toole and the arthritis
text:
It's a Saturday night in Galway, and Paddy O'Toole is coming home from the pub on the last bus. He's had a few. Well, more than a few. His cap is crooked. His tie is over his shoulder. There's lipstick on his collar, and it isn't his wife's shade. He's got the racing form sticking out of his pocket, with three losing horses circled.

He staggers down the aisle and drops into the only empty seat, right next to Father Flanagan.

Paddy pulls a folded-up newspaper from his coat, squints at it for a while, then turns to the priest.

"Father. Can I ask you a question? What causes arthritis?"

Father Flanagan looks him up and down. He's been waiting twenty years for this moment.

"I'll tell you what causes arthritis, Paddy O'Toole. Loose living. Drinking until all hours. Gambling away your wages on the horses. Running around with fast women. Never darkening the door of a church. That's what causes arthritis."

Paddy's eyes go wide. "Well, I'll be."

He goes quiet and stares out the window for the rest of the ride.

The bus pulls up at Paddy's stop. Father Flanagan feels a pang of guilt. He was a bit hard on the man. He puts a hand on Paddy's arm.

"Paddy, I'm sorry. I shouldn't have spoken to you like that. Tell me. How long have you had the arthritis?"

Paddy holds up the newspaper.

"Oh, I don't have it, Father. I was just reading here that the Bishop does."

title: Miss Ida Mae and the sermon
text:
At the little Baptist church out on the county road, the most faithful member is Miss Ida Mae. Eighty-four years old. Front pew, right side, every Sunday for sixty years. And every time the preacher says something she agrees with, she lets him know.

This particular Sunday, the preacher is on fire. Sweat on his brow. Bible in the air.

"Brothers and sisters, we have got to stop the drinking!"

Miss Ida Mae waves her hanky. "Amen!"

"We have got to stop the gambling! The card games and the dice and the lottery tickets!"

"Amen! Preach it!"

"We have got to stop the cussing! The taking of the Lord's name in vain!"

"Amen! Amen!"

"We have got to stop the carousing! The running around! The honky-tonks on Saturday night!"

Miss Ida Mae is on her feet now. "Glory! Tell it, preacher! AMEN!"

The preacher pounds the pulpit. "And we have got to stop the dipping of snuff!"

Miss Ida Mae freezes. She slowly sits back down. She reaches into her pocketbook and feels for the little round tin of snuff she's carried every day since 1958.

She turns to the lady next to her and mutters,

"Well. Now he's done quit preaching and gone to meddling."

title: Farmer Brown's fiftieth anniversary
text:
It's Farmer Brown and Mrs. Brown's fiftieth wedding anniversary. The whole county turns out. There's a big party in the church fellowship hall. Cake, punch, a slide show of fifty years of pictures. The preacher says a prayer. The grandchildren sing a song. Everybody cries.

That night, after the last guest has gone home, Mrs. Brown can't find Farmer Brown anywhere. She looks in the kitchen. The barn. Finally, she finds him out on the back porch, sitting alone in his rocking chair in the dark.

And he's crying. Tears rolling down his cheeks.

Mrs. Brown's heart melts. She sits down beside him and takes his hand. "Oh, Pa. I've never seen you cry. Not in fifty years. Are you that moved? Fifty years together?"

Farmer Brown wipes his eyes. "Ma, do you remember when we were courting? When we were seventeen?"

"Of course I do."

"Do you remember the night your daddy caught us up in the hayloft?"

Mrs. Brown blushes. "Pa! Of course I remember."

"Do you remember how he came up that ladder with his double-barrel shotgun, and pointed it right between my eyes, and said, 'Boy, you are going to marry my daughter, or I am going to have the sheriff lock you up for fifty years'?"

Mrs. Brown smiles softly and squeezes his hand. "I remember, Pa."

Farmer Brown lets out a long, sad sigh and stares out into the dark.

"Well, Ma. Tonight, I'd have been a free man."

title: Farmer Brown's hearing test
text:
Farmer Brown is worried. He's convinced Mrs. Brown is going deaf. He asks her things, and she doesn't answer. He calls her from the barn, and nothing. But he doesn't want to hurt her feelings. So he slips into town to see old Doc Henderson.

"Doc, I think Ma's losing her hearing. But she's proud. She'd never admit it. What do I do?"

Doc Henderson says, "Earl, here's a simple test. Tonight, when she's at the stove, stand about forty feet away and ask her a question in a normal voice. If she doesn't answer, move up to twenty feet and ask again. Then ten feet. Then right behind her. That'll tell us how bad it is."

That evening, Mrs. Brown is in the kitchen, stirring a big pot on the stove. Farmer Brown stands way out at the front door. Forty feet. In a normal voice, he asks,

"Ma, what's for supper?"

Nothing.

He tiptoes down the hall to the dining room. Twenty feet.

"Ma, what's for supper?"

Nothing. Just stirring.

His heart sinks. It's worse than he thought. He creeps up to the kitchen doorway. Ten feet.

"Ma, what's for supper?"

Not a word.

Poor woman. He walks right up behind her, close enough to touch her shoulder, and says gently,

"Ma. What's for supper?"

Mrs. Brown spins around, waving the wooden spoon.

"Pa, for the FOURTH time, CHICKEN AND DUMPLINGS!"

title: Rory's last request
note: Built to test Chip's scale: aimed at an 8.
text:
Years after the three pints, Paddy O'Toole's brothers finally came home. Rory came back from Boston. Finn came back from Sydney. And every night since, the three O'Toole brothers have sat on the same three stools at the end of the bar at Flanagan's. Same stools. Same corner. Same jokes.

One night, Rory sets down his glass and goes quiet.

"Lads. I've been to see the doctor. It's the heart. He gives me a month, maybe two."

Paddy stares at his pint. Finn stares at his. Nobody says a word for a long time.

"Ah, Rory."

"Now listen. I've a last request." Rory points up to the top shelf behind the bar, to a dusty bottle that's been sitting there since 1970. Flanagan's finest. Twenty-five-year-old Irish whiskey. "Paddy, you're the eldest. When I'm gone, I want you to buy that bottle. And I want you to come up to the graveyard, and stand over me, and pour every drop of it on my grave. Will you do that for me?"

Paddy's eyes fill up. He puts a hand on his little brother's shoulder.

"Rory. I'd be honored. I'll do it.

Just one thing. Would you mind if I strained it through my kidneys first?"

title: Before the trouble starts
text:
A man walks into a bar.

It's a quiet Tuesday night. The jukebox is low. A couple of regulars are watching the ballgame. The man sits down at the bar, looks nervously over his shoulder at the door, and says to the bartender,

"Give me a whiskey. Quick. Before the trouble starts."

The bartender pours him a whiskey. The man knocks it back in one gulp. He glances at the door again.

"Give me another one. Quick. Before the trouble starts."

The bartender raises an eyebrow, but he pours another. Down it goes. The man wipes his mouth, looks at the door, looks at the window, and leans in.

"One more. Hurry. Before the trouble starts."

Now the bartender is getting nervous himself. He looks at the door. He looks at the regulars. He eases his hand under the counter, where he keeps the baseball bat. He pours the third whiskey, and the man throws it back.

"Hit me again. Before the trouble starts."

The bartender sets down the bottle.

"Mister, that's four whiskeys. You keep looking at that door. Now I want to know. When exactly is this trouble supposed to start?"

The man sets down his empty glass, sighs, and says,

"Right about now. I haven't got any money."

title: The dog who knows baseball
text:
A man walks into a bar with a scruffy little mutt on a rope leash.

The bartender points at the sign on the wall. "Sorry, pal. No dogs allowed."

"Ah, but this is no ordinary dog," the man says. "This dog can talk. I'll make you a bet. If he talks, you give us free drinks all night. If he doesn't, I'll buy a round for the whole bar."

The regulars perk up. The bartender folds his arms. "All right. Let's hear it."

The man turns to the dog. "Buddy. What's on top of a house?"

The dog looks up and says, "Roof!"

The bartender rolls his eyes. "That's a bark. Every dog in the world says that."

"Hold on, hold on. Buddy, how does sandpaper feel?"

The dog says, "Rough!"

The whole bar groans. The bartender starts coming around the counter.

"Wait! One more! Buddy, who was the greatest baseball player of all time?"

The dog thinks a second and says, "Ruth!"

That's it. The bartender grabs the man by the collar, grabs the dog by the leash, marches them both to the front door, and tosses them out onto the sidewalk.

The man sits there on the curb, rubbing his elbow. The dog sits down next to him, looks up at him, and says,

"DiMaggio?"

title: The horse behind the bar
text:
A man walks into a bar he hasn't been to in about ten years. It's his old hometown watering hole. Same neon sign. Same sticky floor. Same dartboard with the hole in the wall next to it.

He sits down on his old stool, looks up, and freezes.

Behind the bar, wiping down glasses with a towel, is a horse. A big brown horse in a white apron.

The horse sets down the glass and looks at him. "What'll it be?"

The man just stares. His mouth is open. He can't say a word.

The horse sighs. "Look, buddy. I get this every day. What's the matter? Haven't you ever seen a horse tend bar before?"

The man shakes his head slowly.

"It's not that.

I just never thought the cow would sell the place."

title: The kangaroo's change
text:
A man walks into a bar. Right behind him, a kangaroo hops in, climbs up onto the stool next to him, and orders a beer.

The bartender blinks. But business is business. He pours the beer and sets it down.

The kangaroo reaches into his pouch, pulls out a twenty, and slides it across the bar. The bartender figures a kangaroo won't know the price of a beer. He rings it up and slides back one dollar in change.

The kangaroo sips his beer. The bartender keeps wiping the same glass, staring. Finally, he can't help himself.

"You know, we don't get many kangaroos in here."

The kangaroo looks at the dollar bill in front of him, looks back up at the bartender, and says,

"At these prices, I'm not surprised."

title: The snail at the door
text:
A man walks into a bar. It's his bar. He just bought it, and tonight is his very first night as the owner. He's behind the counter, polishing glasses, nervous and proud.

Around closing time, he hears a little tap, tap, tap at the front door. He opens it and looks down. It's a snail.

The snail says, "Evening. Could I get a beer?"

The man is in no mood. Long day. First night. He winds up and kicks that snail as hard as he can, clear across the parking lot and into the weeds. He slams the door and goes back to his glasses.

Two years go by. Business is good. The bar is a success.

One night, around closing time, the man hears a little tap, tap, tap at the front door. He opens it and looks down.

It's the snail. Covered in dust. Shell a little scuffed. And he says,

"What was THAT all about?"

title: The duck who wants grapes
text:
A man walks into a bar and takes a seat at the end. A minute later, a duck waddles in, hops up onto the stool next to him, and says to the bartender,

"Got any grapes?"

The bartender says, "No. This is a bar. We don't have grapes."

The duck hops down and waddles out.

Next night, the man is back on his stool. In comes the duck. Hops up. "Got any grapes?"

"No! I told you yesterday. We don't have any grapes."

The duck waddles out.

Third night. Same man, same stool. In comes the duck. "Got any grapes?"

The bartender slams down his towel. "Listen, you! For the last time, we do not have grapes! If you come in here one more time asking for grapes, I'm going to nail your little webbed feet to this bar!"

The duck waddles out. The man at the end of the bar sips his drink and waits.

Fourth night. In comes the duck. Hops up on the stool, looks the bartender right in the eye, and says,

"Got any nails?"

The bartender says, "No."

The duck says, "Got any grapes?"

title: The complimentary peanuts
text:
A man walks into a bar after the worst day of his life. Lost a big client. Got a parking ticket. Spilled coffee on his only good suit. He drops onto a stool and orders a beer.

The bartender sets it down and goes to the back room to change a keg. The man is alone at the bar.

Then he hears a little voice. "Hey. Nice tie."

He looks around. Nobody there.

"Seriously. That's a great tie. And you've clearly been working out."

He looks down. The voice is coming from the bowl of peanuts on the bar.

"And that suit," says the peanuts. "Very sharp. Very distinguished. Has anyone ever told you that you look a little like Gregory Peck?"

The man is stunned. But honestly, it's the nicest thing anyone's said to him all day. He starts to smile.

Then, from across the room, a gravelly voice. "Hey, you! Yeah, you, loser! Nice coffee stain! What's the matter, couldn't afford a bib? You look like something the cat dragged in!"

The man spins around. It's the cigarette machine in the corner.

Just then, the bartender comes back. The man grabs him by the sleeve. "What on earth is going on in this place? The peanuts are telling me I'm wonderful, and the cigarette machine is calling me a loser!"

The bartender nods and goes back to drying glasses.

"Oh, don't mind them. The peanuts are complimentary.

And the cigarette machine is out of order."

title: The worst day of his life
text:
A man walks into a bar, sits down at the end, and orders a whiskey. Then he just stares at it. He doesn't touch it. He doesn't move. Five minutes. Ten minutes. Half an hour. Just sits there, staring into that glass.

A big trucker at the next stool has been watching him. Six foot four. Tattoos. Mean as a snake. He figures he'll have a little fun. He reaches over, picks up the man's whiskey, and drinks it down in one gulp. Then he slams the empty glass on the bar and grins.

The little man puts his face in his hands and starts to cry.

The trucker feels bad. "Aw, come on, buddy. I was just kidding around. I'll buy you another one. I can't stand to see a man cry."

The man shakes his head. "No, it's not you. It's just been the worst day of my life.

"This morning, I overslept, so I was late for work. My boss fired me on the spot. I walked out to the parking lot, and my car had been stolen. The police said there's nothing they can do. So I took a cab home, and as the cab drove off, I realized I'd left my wallet in the back seat. I walked into my house, and there was my wife, with the mailman. I walked out, and I came here.

"And just as I'm working up the courage to put an end to it all, sitting here, staring at the glass I just poured the poison into...

"You come along and drink it."

title: Thirty days
note: Claude's best shot at a 10 on Chip's scale.
text:
A man walks into a bar and sits down heavily on the end stool. Gray suit. Loosened tie. Shoulders slumped like he's carrying a piano on his back. He orders a double bourbon and stares into it.

The bartender has seen this look a thousand times. He leans on the bar. "Rough day, friend?"

The man sighs. "Rough month."

"Want to talk about it?"

The man turns the glass slowly on the bar. "Thirty-one years I've been married. Thirty-one years. A month ago, my wife and I had the worst fight we've ever had. I said some things. She said some things. And at the end of it, she looked me dead in the eye and said, 'Harold, I am not going to speak to you for thirty days.'"

The bartender winces. "Thirty days? Not one word?"

"Not one word. Not good morning. Not good night. Not pass the salt. Not one single word for thirty days."

"Oh, man. I'm sorry. That's terrible."

The man nods slowly. He picks up the bourbon, takes a long swallow, sets the glass down, and stares at the clock on the wall.

"Yep. And tonight's the thirtieth."

title: The alligator orders
text:
A man walks into a bar in downtown Atlanta with a twelve-foot alligator on a leash.

Not a little one. A full-grown Okefenokee swamp gator. Four hundred pounds. Tail sweeping the barstools over like bowling pins. Teeth like a row of steak knives. It drags its belly across the floor, leaving a long wet streak, and every man in the place climbs up onto the pool table.

The man sits down at the bar. The alligator settles in next to him, swishes its tail, and knocks the jukebox off the wall.

The bartender is pressed flat against the liquor shelf. He's holding a bottle of gin like a club. His voice comes out about two octaves high.

"Mister. Can I... help you?"

The man folds his hands on the bar, calm as a deacon. "Just one question. Do you serve lawyers here?"

The bartender blinks. "Lawyers? Well... yes. Sure. We serve lawyers. Half the courthouse drinks here."

The man nods. "Good.

I'll have a beer. And my alligator will have a lawyer."
note: Chip: "That was horrible." Lawyer put-down misses his taste.

title: The parrot's answer
text:
A man walks into a bar with the most magnificent parrot anyone has ever seen, perched on his shoulder.

A giant scarlet macaw. Three feet from beak to tail. Feathers of red and gold and electric blue. It looks like it flew straight out of a museum painting. Every head in the room turns. Somebody drops a pool cue.

The bartender comes over slowly, staring. "My Lord. That is the most beautiful creature I've ever seen in my life. Where on earth did you get him?"

The parrot looks the bartender up and down. Ruffles its feathers. And says,

"Jacksonville. They've got thousands of 'em down there."

title: Farmer Brown and Ma's cat
text:
A man walks into a bar. It's Farmer Brown, on his one night a year in town. He drops onto a stool, looking like he's been through a war, and orders a double.

The bartender knows him. "Earl. What happened to you?"

Farmer Brown sighs. "Ma's cat."

"Her cat?"

"Fourteen years, that cat has lived in my house. Sleeps in my chair. Sheds on my good suit. Sharpens its claws on my boots. Ma loves that cat more than she loves me. And I can't stand the sight of it.

"So Monday, while Ma was at her quilting circle, I put that cat in a feed sack, put the sack in the truck, drove five miles down the county road, and let it out by the creek. I drove home. And when I pulled into the yard, there was the cat, sitting on the porch, licking its paw.

"Tuesday, I drove it fifteen miles, clear across the county line. Got home. Cat's on the porch.

"Wednesday, I drove it thirty miles, over the river, into the next county. Got home. Cat's on the porch. Looking at me.

"So today, I'd had enough. I put that cat in the truck, and I drove. Fifty miles. Turned left. Turned right. Over the mountain. Down the dirt roads. Back roads. Logging roads. Left, right, left, left, right, until I didn't know north from Sunday. And I let that cat out in the middle of the woods."

The bartender says, "Well, that's it, then. You finally got rid of it."

Farmer Brown shakes his head.

"Not exactly. About an hour later, I had to call Ma on the telephone and ask her if the cat was home yet.

She said yes.

I said, 'Put him on the phone. I'm lost.'"

title: The trader at the Pearly Gates
note: Aimed at a 9 on Chip's scale.
text:
A legendary Wall Street trader dies and arrives at the Pearly Gates. Forty years on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange. Made fortunes. Lost fortunes. Made them back.

Saint Peter looks him up in the book and frowns. "Well, your record's acceptable. Barely. But I'm afraid I can't let you in. We have a section up here reserved for Wall Street people, and it's full. Packed. Not one seat left. I'm sorry."

The trader thinks for a moment. "Saint Peter, I'll make you a deal. Let me just stick my head in the gate and say four words to the boys. That's all. Four words. Then I'll go quietly."

Saint Peter shrugs. "Four words. Go ahead."

The trader leans through the gate, cups his hands around his mouth, and shouts,

"OIL DISCOVERED IN HELL!"

There's a roar. A stampede. Thousands of traders, brokers, bankers, and fund managers come pouring out of the Wall Street section. Robes flying. Halos bouncing. Elbowing each other out of the way. They rush right past Saint Peter, out the gate, and dive straight down toward the fire and brimstone.

In thirty seconds, the Wall Street section is empty.

Saint Peter is impressed. "Well, I'll be. That was very clever. Come on in. You can have any seat you like."

The trader doesn't move. He's staring down after them. He scratches his chin.

"No, thanks, Saint Peter. I think I'll go along with the rest of the boys.

There might be something to that rumor."

title: The magician and the parrot
note: Aimed at a 9 on Chip's scale. Animal joke.
text:
The Great Zambini is a magician on a cruise ship. Twice a night, every night, in the ship's lounge. Card tricks. Disappearing coins. Pulling doves out of a top hat. It's not the big time, but it's steady work, and the audience changes every week, so he never needs new material.

There's just one problem. The captain's parrot.

The parrot lives in a brass cage right next to the stage. And after three years of watching the same show, twice a night, that parrot knows every trick by heart. And he can't keep his beak shut.

Zambini makes a card disappear. The parrot squawks, "It's up his sleeve! It's up his sleeve!"

Zambini pulls a coin out of a lady's ear. "It was in his other hand! Other hand!"

Zambini makes a dove vanish. "Trap door in the hat! Trap door in the hat!"

The audience roars. Zambini smiles through gritted teeth. Night after night. Year after year. He hates that bird with every fiber of his being.

Then one night, in the middle of the North Atlantic, during the big finale, the ship hits an iceberg. There's a tremendous crash. The lights go out. The ship rolls over and sinks in minutes.

When the sun comes up, there's nothing left on the ocean but a single wooden plank. And on that plank, soaking wet, are the Great Zambini and the parrot.

They drift for a day. Neither one says a word.

They drift for two days. The parrot just stares at him.

They drift for three days. Not a word. Just that bird, staring, staring.

On the fourth morning, the parrot finally ruffles his wet feathers, leans in close, and says,

"All right. I give up. What did you do with the ship?"

title: Farmer Brown's three-legged chickens
text:
A traveling salesman is driving down the county road past Farmer Brown's place, doing about fifty miles an hour. He glances out the window, and he nearly drives into the ditch.

Running right alongside his car, keeping pace, is a chicken. A chicken with three legs.

He speeds up to sixty. The chicken speeds up to sixty. He hits seventy. The chicken passes him, cuts across the road in front of him, and darts down Farmer Brown's driveway.

The salesman slams on the brakes, turns in, and follows it all the way up to the barn. There's Farmer Brown, leaning on the fence. And behind him, scratching around the barnyard, are about two hundred chickens. Every last one of them with three legs.

"Mister, I just clocked one of your chickens at seventy miles an hour. And it's got three legs!"

Farmer Brown nods. "Yep. I breed 'em that way."

"Why on earth would you breed a three-legged chicken?"

"Well, it's like this. There's me, there's Ma, and there's our boy Junior. And all three of us like the drumstick. Every Sunday supper, there's a fight. So I spent twelve years crossbreeding, and I finally got me a chicken with three legs. A drumstick for everybody."

The salesman shakes his head in wonder. "That's incredible. So tell me. How do they taste?"

Farmer Brown spits in the dirt.

"Couldn't tell you. Ain't caught one yet."
note: Chip: "the punchline was weak." Score is Claude's revised guess, not Chip's number.
